content: I liked it. Before approving, I'd like to know how similar a contribution can be to another to not get rejected because after the author's update, this contribution looks very similar to this one: https://www.codingame.com/contribute/view/1371637e68d6d4e6eebd3286c57c4b63e1b71f
I tweaked it a little bit and added a condition. I dont know if that makes it better

This clash feels a bit too similar to https://www.codingame.com/contribute/view/1371637e68d6d4e6eebd3286c57c4b63e1b71f. I get that the output is different, but the concept is identical.

While waiting for other reviewers to chime in, please fix the following formatting issues:

- Please format "NONE" (in the Output section) as {{NONE}}.

- Please format "n" and "h" (in the Constraints section) as [[n]] and [[h]].

- Please use suitable ranges for n and h that closely match your test cases. Alternatively, please create more tests/validators that have more heights (greater n), and/or more varied height values (inclusive of negative values, though I'm not sure how that works).

- Please change the second line of the stub generator input to: loopline n h:int
I guess I will think of something else then. It seems very similar to the other one. Thank you
Didn't see @User123 pointed this out already. If it's good for them, then I'm happy to approve.

Just in case you decide to keep this contribution, below are a few points to follow up. Otherwise, please consider them as a reference for your future contributions:

Goal
* Please change "numbers"/"number" to "integers"/"integer".

* Please change "print" to "output".

Input
* Line 2: Please change "numbers" to "integers representing the heights of a mountain range".

Output
* Please change "Print all" to "<<Line 1:>> All".

Cases
* Test 3: Please change the input to use 3-digit integers for all [[h]].

* Please add Test 5 and Validator 5, where the input is a strictly decreasing sequence consisting of 1-digit, 2-digit and 3-digit integers.

Thanks.
You could add something to process, like give values in either meters or feet, so f.e. Mt. Everest is given as either 	8,848.86 m  or 29,031.7 ft.

The author's new idea of the revised contribution is good, but the cases need to be improved and expanded.

Game modes
* It may be too difficult to infer the task from the visible test cases alone in Reverse mode.

Constraints
* Please relax the upper bound of n to 20.

Cases
* Please avoid using too many 1-digit heights in the cases. Instead, revise them as follows:

  • Test/Validator 2: Use 2-digit heights.

  • Test/Validator 3: Use 3-digit heights.

  • Test/Validator 4 and onwards: Use a mix of 1-digit, 2-digit and 3-digit heights.

* Test 4: Please revise the case so that N = 8 and k > 10, similar to Validator 4.

* Please add the following new pairs of cases:

  • N = 1.

  • N = 2.

  • A non-strictly increasing sequence of heights containing all possible differences between consecutive heights: 0, less than k, equal to k and greater than k.

  • A non-strictly decreasing sequence of heights containing all possible differences between consecutive heights: 0, less than k, equal to k and greater than k.

  • N = 10, k > 30, and every peak is exactly k higher than its neighbours.

  • N = 15, k > 60, and covering all the following combinations:
    - a peak exactly k higher than both neighbours.
    - a peak exactly k higher than the left neighbour and more than k higher than the right neighbour.
    - a peak more than k higher than the left neighbour and exactly k higher than the right neighbour.

  • N = 20, k > 90 with all combinations:
    - all combinations listed for N = 15.
    - a height lower than both neighbours.
    - a height exactly k higher than the left neighbour but lower than the right neighbour.
    - a height exactly k higher than the right neighbour but lower than the left neighbour.
    - the leftmost height at least k higher than the second height.
    - the rightmost height at least k higher than the second-last height.

Thanks.
